node.label: Sherry Olson
node.date_label: 'Baltimore Imitates the Spider' 1979 · Baltimore: The Building of an American City 1980 · 'Occupations and Residential Spaces' 1989 · 'Le peuplement de Montréal' 1997 · MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé, from 2000 · Peopling the North American City (with Patricia Thornton) 2011 · 'Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal' (with Dufaux) 2014
node.description: A historical geographer, at Johns Hopkins and then McGill, whose Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980) is 'about city building', read as 'a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks'. In Montreal she and her collaborators, among them the demographer Patricia Thornton, followed sampled families through parish registers, censuses and municipal taxrolls and mapped them; her 1997 chapter for the Atlas historique du Québec, mapped with GIS at McGill, sets out to 'saisir … les processus par lesquels la cité se construit'. With Robert Sweeny, Jason Gilliland and others she built MAP (Montréal, l'avenir du passé, begun in 2000), a collective historical GIS in which, as she and François Dufaux wrote in 2014, 'the spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot'. The editors of Historical GIS Research in Canada (2014) name MAP, 'led by' Olson and Sweeny, among the few Canadian HGIS projects since the 1990s, and a Victoria team that includes Gilliland calls her Montreal work 'a model of spatial history'; Sweeny, MAP's co-director, warned in 2009 that 'the ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding'. With Thornton she wrote Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011), which, by its publisher's description, follows families of twelve surnames.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Sherry H. Olson; The Depletion Myth: A History of Railroad Use of Timber (1971); “Baltimore Imitates the Spider” (Annals of the AAG, 1979); Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980; bicentennial edition 1997); with Patricia Thornton and Quoc Thuy Thach, “Dimensions sociales de la mortalité infantile à Montréal au milieu du XIXe siècle” (Annales de démographie historique, 1989); “Occupations and Residential Spaces in Nineteenth-Century Montreal” (Historical Methods, 1989); with David Hanna, “The Social Landscape of Montréal, 1901” (Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 3, plate 30, 1990); “Le peuplement de Montréal” (Atlas historique du Québec: Population et territoire, 1997); with Jason Gilliland, “Claims on Housing Space in Nineteenth-Century Montreal” (Urban History Review, 1998). After 2000: MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé (from 2000, with Robert Sweeny and others); “Ethnic Partition of the Work Force in 1840s Montréal” (Labour/Le Travail, 2004); with Gilliland, “Residential Segregation in the Industrializing City” (Urban Geography, 2010); with Gilliland and Danielle Gauvreau, “Did Segregation Increase as the City Expanded?” (Social Science History, 2011); with Patricia Thornton, Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011); with François Dufaux, “Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal” (2014). Readings: Sweeny (2009); Sager (2012); Horner (2013); Bonnell and Fortin (2014); Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014).
node.scope_note: A method entry for historical GIS, not a Quebec-historiography entry: the Quebec self-accounts read for the atlas (Ouellet 1985, Bédard, Bouchard, Rudin, Savard, Linteau) do not name her. Her own words are read in the introduction and acknowledgments of Baltimore (1980), in full in 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (1997), in part in the 2004 Labour/Le Travail research note, and in part in her 2014 chapter with Dufaux; the 1979, 1998, 2010 and 2011 articles are known from their abstracts, and the 1989 Historical Methods article and the 1990 atlas plate at title level only. Peopling the North American City is unread; it is known from publisher copy and the opening paragraphs of Sager's (2012) and Horner's (2013) reviews. In-period reviews of Baltimore exist (AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture, JEH 1981; JIH, Journal of Historical Geography 1982) but were not readable here. The GIS work begins in the 1990s; MAP dates from 2000 and is collective, co-led with Robert Sweeny, whose team built the electronic framework from the Cane map of 1846. She is not presented as the founder of HGIS in Canada: 'pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, and the editors of the 2014 volume list national repositories in the United States and Britain as 'some of the most important work in the field'. The 2014 volume's chapter 2 (Beard, Macfarlane and Clifford) is not used.

incident_edges.relationship: Households placed on the urban lot: linked parish, census and tax records for nineteenth-century Montreal, mapped with GIS at McGill in the 1990s and built from 2000 into the collective MAP geodatabase
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (Atlas historique du Québec, 1997; read in full) works from 'l’exemple local pour ensuite faire ressortir la vue d’ensemble et saisir ainsi, dans une démarche exploratoire, les processus par lesquels la cité se construit' (p. 81). Its samples are built from records, and differ by population: the Catholic baptismal cohort of 1859, whose parents were traced through the Drouin index and the Notre-Dame registers (n. 4); for the Protestant population only, a micro-sample of ten surnames ('Pour la population protestante, notre microéchantillon s’appuie sur dix patronymes', p. 85), distinct from the twelve-surname sampling that the publisher's description gives for the later book with Thornton (2011, unread here); a 'Montréal « miniaturisé »' of 370 household heads in 1900, and building tradesmen from the 'rôle d’évaluation' plotted in half-kilometre rings 'à la manière d’une reconstitution cinématographique' (p. 89). Note 1 credits the demographic analysis to Patricia Thornton and the mapping 'sur ATLAS GIS' to Ben Johnson and Ingrid Olson, with the McGill GIS laboratory. Earlier work is known only at title level ('Occupations and Residential Spaces', Historical Methods, 1989) or from an abstract (with Gilliland, Urban History Review, 1998: 'From small samples of the Montreal population over the years 1861-1901'). After 2000, her own words. In 2004 she describes the method and its limits: cross-referencing the 1842 census, the 1848 directory and the 1848 taxroll 'in an iterative process of matching surnames, first names, streets of residence, and occupations'; of 5,192 taxroll entries '75 per cent can be matched to the directory, 45 per cent to the census 5 years earlier, and 41 per cent to both sources' (Labour/Le Travail 53, pp. 173–74). In the same note Robert Sweeny 'has created from the Cane map an electronic framework' (p. 165, note). With Dufaux (2014): MAP is 'a collective project in which dozens of people have invested their skills'; 'The spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot – 7,000 lots in the 1850s, 30,000 in 1900' (p. 155); 'A dozen Montreal scholars and a dozen graduate students initiated the project in 2000' (p. 176 n. 1). From abstracts: the 2010 and 2011 papers with Gilliland (and Gauvreau) locate '17,000 individual households' in 1881 and re-aggregate lots into 'districts with identical boundaries for both years', 'overcoming the major methodological problems hindering previous comparative analyses'. Reception (later readings, labelled). Bonnell and Fortin (2014, p. xii): 'Since the 1990s, only a small number of historical geographers and historians have used GIS technology' in Canada; 'Notable projects include Montréal, l’avenir du passé, a comprehensive HGIS database of Montreal led by McGill geographer Sherry Olson and Memorial University historian Robert Sweeny'; 'Olson, Sweeny, and Gilliland’s work has captured the interest of a new generation of graduate students and new scholars' (p. xiii). Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014, p. 11): 'we are following the lead of Sherry Olson, whose pioneering work on nineteenth-century Montreal is a model of spatial history'; their n. 31 lists her 'foundational studies'. That chapter is not independent: Gilliland was her MAP collaborator. Contested: Sweeny, MAP's co-director (Digital Studies, 2009), argues that 'The ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding', that a GIS ensures 'the illusion of accuracy', and that 'an historical GIS works because it is a-historical'. This is a critique of the instrument from inside the project, not of Olson. Not a founding: the editors give the US and British national repositories as 'some of the most important work in the field' (p. xi), and the strand's Gregory and Southall (1998) is a separate, aggregate-boundary tradition. 'Pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, not this entry's.

incident_edges.relationship: City building in long swings: Baltimore's growth read through cycles of investment, construction and neighbourhood change (1979–80), and Montreal's through its builders and migrants (1997–2011)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. Baltimore (1980; introduction and acknowledgments read): 'There is a tempo and a pattern to urban growth'; 'City growth is a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks. This applies equally to North America and Europe over at least two centuries'; 'This book is about city building, an internal dynamic of the city-state, and how Baltimoreans see themselves and their situation. In that sense, Baltimore is America, in its rhythm of building up and tearing down, swarming and dispersing' (pp. ix–x). She names what the book leaves out: 'The most serious gap is our ignorance of the lives of slaves and servants in Baltimore', the Polish Catholic community, and 'the strategies of landowners and real estate investors in each round' (pp. ix–x). The acknowledgments record that 'David Harvey shared his discovery of Baltimore for several years' (p. vii). The 1979 Annals article (abstract only): 'The long-swing rhythm of urban investment has produced distinctive spaces and forms in the city', with 'a tempo and a spatial matrix for income redistribution, social conflict, and social pathology'. Montreal (1997, read in full): migration 'Récurrentes de 20 ans en 20 ans' (p. 81); half the population lived within a kilometre of the centre in 1861, in the next ring by 1881 and the one beyond by 1901, as the building trades, 'telle une vague déferlante, se déplacent vers la périphérie' (p. 89). Reception. In-period reviews of Baltimore appeared in the AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture and JEH (1981) and in JIH and the Journal of Historical Geography (1982); none could be read here (JSTOR, OUP and Elsevier walls; the JEH first-page preview image was illegible), so no in-period judgement is reported. Later readings, snippet witnesses (opening paragraphs only): Sager (CHR, 2012) reads Peopling the North American City (2011, unread here) as 'an example of the research collaboratory that has emerged in recent decades'; Horner (HS/SH, 2013) says it 'makes a vital contribution not only to the historiography of Montreal and Quebec, but also to the way that historians and geographers conceptualize the relationship between individuals, families, communities and urban space'. A contribution to the field's building-and-space strand beside Warner, not a new school.

records.context: Places sampled and linked households (parish registers, censuses, taxrolls) on the streets and lots of nineteenth-century Montreal: mapped with GIS at McGill in the 1990s, then built with Robert Sweeny and others into the collective MAP geodatabase from 2000. The 2014 Canadian HGIS volume names MAP among the few Canadian HGIS projects since the 1990s; Sweeny, its co-director, questions GIS as a historical instrument.

sources.title: Sherry H. Olson, Baltimore: The Building of an American City (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1980).
sources.citation: Sherry H. Olson, Baltimore: The Building of an American City (Baltimore and London: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1980), xiii, 432 pp. LCCN 79-21950; ISBN 0-8018-2224-6. Revised and expanded bicentennial edition, 1997.

verification.note: Front matter read in the Maryland State Archives electronic edition (megafile/ecp/26/037, file olson00.html: copyright page, contents, acknowledgments p. vii, introduction pp. ix–x; the HTML gives no page break inside the introduction, so introduction quotations are cited as pp. ix–x). Chapter text not read. Quoted: 'There is a tempo and a pattern to urban growth'; 'City growth is a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks. This applies equally to North America and Europe over at least two centuries, and to much of the world in the last hundred years'; 'This book is about city building, an internal dynamic of the city-state, and how Baltimoreans see themselves and their situation. In that sense, Baltimore is America, in its rhythm of building up and tearing down, swarming and dispersing'; the gaps she names: 'The most serious gap is our ignorance of the lives of slaves and servants in Baltimore', the Polish Catholic community, and 'the strategies of landowners and real estate investors in each round'; 'the city's social record is built into its dwellings' (pp. ix–x). Acknowledgments (p. vii): 'David Harvey shared his discovery of Baltimore for several years'; 'six cohorts of undergraduate students at Johns Hopkins University'. Contents: eleven chapters periodised from 'The Empty Century' to 'Hemmed In, 1935-1979'. The MSA text is a transcription; one OCR capital ('Separating') is silently lower-cased.

sources.scope_note: Her own in-period statement of city building in long swings. Introduction and acknowledgments only.

Quoted: she uses 'the 1842 manuscript census to estimate the relative sizes of four cultural communities and the social distances among them' (p. 159); the census's 'street-by-street organization, in conjunction with the detailed 1846 map of surveyor James Cane, provides cues to residential patterns' (p. 165); a note on p. 165 (n. 32 by the note sequence): 'In a joint program with a dozen scholars, Robert Sweeny (Memorial University of Newfoundland) has created from the Cane map an electronic framework, and we anticipate further analysis of the spatial occupancy'; 'I have in fact cross-referenced the three sources—the census of 1842, the city directory of 1848, and the taxroll of 1848—in an iterative process of matching surnames, first names, streets of residence, and occupations. verification.note: Repository abstract as held by OpenAlex; the repository URL now redirects to the new Memorial repository home page, so the record itself was not seen and its date is uncertain (it describes later layers in the present tense). Abstract: 'Montréal l'avenir du passé (MAP) was established in 2000 to create an historical GIS research infrastructure for 19th and 20th century Montréal. It consists of six highly detailed digitized historical maps representing all buildings in the city for 1825, 1846, 1880, 1912, 1949 and 2000. The first three and last have been geo-referenced and they have been "peopled" by linking at the street-scape (1846) or lot level (1880 & 2000) census returns, tax records, city directories and a wide variety of non-routinely generated sources.'

Nous le ferons en utilisant l’exemple local pour ensuite faire ressortir la vue d’ensemble et saisir ainsi, dans une démarche exploratoire, les processus par lesquels la cité se construit'; migration 'Récurrentes de 20 ans en 20 ans' (p. 81); 'Pour la population protestante, notre microéchantillon s’appuie sur dix patronymes' (p. 85); 'parmi les 370 chefs de ménage du Montréal « miniaturisé » de notre échantillon'; trades from the 'rôle d’évaluation' plotted 'à la manière d’une reconstitution cinématographique', in circles every half-kilometre from the Custom House: half the population within one kilometre of the centre in 1861, in the 1–2 km ring in 1881 and the 2–3 km ring in 1901; builders 'telle une vague déferlante, se déplacent vers la périphérie' (p. 89). Note 1: Patricia Thornton (Concordia) is associated 'pour toutes les analyses démographiques' and David Hanna for construction data; 'Ben Johnson et Ingrid Olson ont effectué la cartographie sur ATLAS GIS, et Lilian Lee a fourni l’assistance technique du laboratoire SIG de l’Université McGill'; 'Jason Gilliland a contribué à l’analyse des loyers et de la mobilité'. Note 4: birthplaces of the 1859 baptismal cohort's parents traced through the Drouin marriage index and the Notre-Dame registers.

sources.scope_note: Her own in-period (1997) account of a sampled, mapped and record-linked Montreal, made with GIS at McGill.

verification.note: Author abstract only (OpenAlex record of the DOI; body closed): 'The long-swing rhythm of urban investment has produced distinctive spaces and forms in the city. The timing and spatial structure of city-building also created a tempo and a spatial matrix for income redistribution, social conflict, and social pathology. Baltimore, Maryland, illustrates the persistence of such patterns for two centuries. The geographical strategies of Baltimore investors, 1865 to 1878, reveal the connections among several types of urban investment and among various parts of the urban landscape.'

Quoted: MAP was 'a collaboration between geographers and historians'; 'Each layer consists of an historical map dynamically linked to a variety of period sources'; 'All the joys and the frustrations of data entry, warping, proofing, linkage, and analysis were shared'; 'The ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding'; 'A GIS mobilizes centuries of cartographic conventions with the latest in computer technologies to ensure the illusion of accuracy'; 'Accurate rectifications required an almost exclusive reliance on property lines as our anchoring, reference points.
